opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to first be clear about what the limitation actually is, because people often frame it as an architectural detail, as if a better attention mechanism or a longer context window will fix it. I don't think that's the case.

The core issue is that a transformer, like any deep learning model trained with gradient descent, is fundamentally a big parametric curve. It's fitted to a data distribution, and what you get at the end is a continuous, interpolative mapping from inputs to outputs. That's extremely powerful when you're operating within the training distribution, which is why these models look so impressive. They've basically memorized a vast library of patterns and templates, and they can retrieve and recombine them fluidly. But that's a different thing from generalization in the sense I care about: the ability to deal with novelty, situations you weren't prepared for, by synthesizing a new solution on the fly.

So could you change the architecture to fix that? You can certainly make incremental improvements. Better inductive biases, better ways of handling compositionality, maybe some forms of recurrence. These will move the needle a little. But as long as the paradigm is "fit a static curve to a giant dataset, then do inference by a single forward pass," you're still doing a form of interpolation. You're still limited to what was in the training data, in a slightly more abstract space.

What I think is actually needed is a shift in the paradigm itself, not just the architecture. Specifically, you need test-time adaptation: the ability to do some kind of search or program synthesis at inference time, to actually construct a new model of the problem in front of you rather than just retrieving one. And you need to combine the two kinds of abstraction. Deep learning is very good at what I call value-centric abstraction, the continuous, intuitive, perception-like kind of pattern matching. But it's very bad at program-centric abstraction, discrete, compositional, symbolic reasoning, where you're recombining building blocks to fit a new situation exactly.

The way forward, in my view, is a hybrid: use deep learning as the intuition engine that guides a discrete program search, so you can tame the combinatorial explosion, and use program synthesis to get the kind of strong, out-of-distribution generalization that curve-fitting can't give you. And we've actually seen evidence for this. The approaches that made real progress on ARC were the ones that introduced test-time training or test-time search, not the ones that just scaled up a bigger transformer.

So, to answer directly: I'm skeptical that architecture changes alone will get you there. The bottleneck isn't the shape of the network. It's the fact that the system is static at inference time. Once you make it able to adapt and recombine on the fly, that's where you start seeing genuine fluid intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't believe the generalization problem is fundamentally an architecture problem. People have been trying to fix it at the architecture level for years now — adding recurrence back in, adding external memory, adding adaptive computation time, various forms of sparsity — and what you tend to see is that these changes buy you something on specific benchmarks, but they don't change the basic character of what the model is doing. It's still curve fitting. It's still interpolating between points in a very high-dimensional space defined by the training data.

The limitation that I care about is the inability to adapt to genuine novelty — to a situation that is not just a recombination of things you've seen before at the surface level. And that limitation comes from the learning paradigm, not from the shape of the network. A transformer is a very good differentiable program for turning a large static dataset into a continuous model of the data manifold. That's what gradient descent gives you. If you change the architecture but you keep the paradigm — big parametric model, trained once, then frozen, then queried — you're still going to end up with something that can only handle inputs that are close to its training distribution.

So when people ask me, "is there an architectural fix," my honest answer is that I think it's the wrong framing. If you want to overcome this, I think you need a different kind of program synthesis, something that does discrete search over programs at test time, not just a forward pass. Deep learning is extremely good at perception, at pattern recognition, at intuition. What it's bad at is reasoning, the kind of step-by-step, compositional recombination of known building blocks into a new program that fits a problem you've never seen. And those are two different things that I believe require two different kinds of machinery.

Now, that doesn't mean architecture is irrelevant. There are things you can do to make models better at reusing knowledge, better at modularity — and I do think some of the recent work on test-time training, test-time search, program-synthesis-flavored approaches on ARC, is actually interesting precisely because it moves away from the frozen-model paradigm. But I would describe those as changes in how you use the model, not changes in the model. The architecture is almost incidental.

So to assess the possibility: I think if you stay inside the transformer paradigm and just modify the architecture, you'll keep getting incremental gains and you'll keep hitting the same wall. If you're willing to step outside that paradigm and build hybrid systems — deep learning for intuition and perception, discrete search for reasoning — then I think the limitation is very much overcomeable. That's what I'm actually optimistic about.

astra-6.text:
I think architecture changes can help, but I wouldn’t expect architecture alone to solve the problem. You have to ask what kind of generalization you’re talking about. Generalizing to new examples that follow familiar patterns is quite different from adapting to a genuinely new task, where the relevant patterns aren’t already represented in your training experience.

A different architecture can introduce useful inductive biases. It can make certain abstractions easier to learn or certain computations easier to express. But if your approach is still essentially to fit a model to a very large distribution of examples, changing the architecture doesn’t automatically give you the ability to invent an appropriate solution when you encounter something outside that distribution.

What I find more promising is combining learned intuition with explicit search and composition. You can use a neural network to guide the process, but you also need some way to construct and test new solutions at inference time. Program synthesis is one way to think about that: taking reusable pieces of knowledge and assembling them into a program for a problem you haven’t seen before.

So I wouldn’t say transformers are a dead end. They can be very useful components. But overcoming their generalization limitations may require changing the overall approach to learning and problem-solving, rather than simply replacing attention with another mechanism.

sol-6.1.text:
I think architecture changes can help, but I don’t think there’s a particular architectural tweak that will suddenly give us general intelligence. The more fundamental question is: what mechanism allows a system to adapt to a problem that wasn’t anticipated by its training data?

Transformers are very good at learning patterns across a large distribution of examples. But improving that ability isn’t necessarily the same as improving the ability to invent a new solution when those patterns no longer apply. You can make the model larger or change how attention works, and you may push the boundary considerably. That doesn’t establish that you’ve solved the underlying generalization problem.

What I would look for is a system that can construct and test new abstractions at inference time. Program synthesis is one possible approach: you use learned knowledge to guide a search, but the solution itself can be a new composition of things you already know. Deep learning could be a very powerful component of that system.

So I’m open to architectural innovation. But I would assess it by whether it introduces a meaningful capacity for adaptation, and whether that capacity holds up on genuinely novel problems—not simply by whether it improves performance on another familiar benchmark.
